lesson.title: Evolving Together: The Logic of Coevolution
lesson.summary: Coevolution occurs when two or more species exert reciprocal natural selection on each other over time, so that an evolutionary change in one species changes the relative fitness landscape for the other, driving the two lineages to adapt in tandem.
lesson.body:
Coevolution describes a specific kind of evolutionary relationship in which two species act as persistent selective forces on each other, so that each one's evolutionary trajectory is shaped, generation after generation, by changes happening in the other. This builds directly on natural selection and relative fitness: recall that relative fitness measures how well a particular trait or genotype performs compared to others in the same population, not in some absolute sense, and that natural selection favors whatever raises relative fitness given the current environment. Coevolution is what happens when a large part of "the current environment" for one species is, quite literally, another species that is itself evolving in response. Each side's adaptation changes the fitness landscape the other side is being selected on, which can set off a continuing back-and-forth over many generations.

Coevolution takes different forms depending on the kind of relationship between the species involved. In mutualistic relationships, where both species benefit, coevolution can produce remarkably tight, sometimes highly specialized partnerships. A classic and very well documented case is the relationship between yucca plants and yucca moths. Female yucca moths are essentially the exclusive pollinators of yucca flowers, gathering pollen and actively packing it onto the flower's stigma, but the moth also lays her eggs in the flower's ovary, and her larvae eat some, but typically not all, of the developing seeds. Each species has evolved traits fitted to the other, the moth to the flower's specific structure and pollination needs, the flower to depend on this reliable pollination service, so that neither the plant nor the moth reproduces well without the other. A second well known and carefully documented mutualistic case involves the orchid Angraecum sesquipedale from Madagascar, whose flowers hold nectar at the bottom of an extraordinarily long, narrow spur. When Darwin examined this flower, he predicted that a pollinator with an equally long tongue must exist to reach the nectar, even though no such insect had yet been found. Decades later, a moth species with a proboscis long enough to match the orchid's spur was in fact discovered, and later observation confirmed it does pollinate the flower. That predicted long-tongued moth is now recognized as a subspecies bearing the name praedicta, a nod to Darwin's prediction, and the orchid-moth pair is widely cited as an example of coevolution driving matching extremes in two interacting species.

Coevolution is just as important, and in some ways easier to see clearly, in antagonistic relationships such as predator and prey or parasite and host, where the two species are locked in what biologists sometimes call an evolutionary arms race: an adaptation that improves one species' relative fitness lowers the other's, which then selects for a counter-adaptation, and so on. One of the most rigorously studied cases involves the rough-skinned newt, which produces a potent neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin in its skin, and the common garter snake, one of the few predators able to eat these newts and survive. Research (much of it by biologists Edmund Brodie Jr. and Edmund Brodie III) tracking newt toxin levels and snake resistance across many populations in the Pacific Northwest of North America found that in areas where garter snakes have evolved strong genetic resistance to the toxin, through mutations affecting the sodium channels the toxin normally blocks, newt populations tend to carry unusually high toxin levels, and where snake resistance is lower, newt toxin levels tend to be lower too. This geographic matching between predator resistance and prey toxicity is exactly what an ongoing reciprocal arms race would be expected to produce, each side's evolutionary response to the other pushing the pair toward more extreme traits in tandem.

The thread connecting both mutualistic and antagonistic coevolution back to relative fitness is worth stating plainly: coevolution does not require that either species is evolving toward some fixed, absolute goal. It only requires that each species' relative fitness depends in part on traits found in the other species, so that a shift in one changes what counts as advantageous in the other. That is also why coevolutionary relationships, whether cooperative or antagonistic, tend to persist and intensify over long stretches of time rather than settling into a permanent, unchanging equilibrium, since each adaptive step by one partner reopens the selective pressure on the other.
